cells.tense: You are here, at the ending, with your hands actually on it.
cells.ask: Say the true thing to one person this week — the one you've been softening — and let how they take it be theirs to manage.
cells.core:
You're in the middle of a real ending, and you're in it awake. You know what has to stop, you've said so to the people it touches, and you're not pretending the clearing is someone else's job. That's the whole thing working. What you carry well is the connection underneath the change — people feel held even as you tell them what's over.

The next move isn't more feeling. It's precision. Bring the same care you use to keep people close to the actual facts of what you're ending, one conversation at a time. When you tell someone the truth and then stay in the room with them, that's the balance holding. It costs something to keep — you don't get to make it painless — but it's yours to spend.
cells.sheetLine: You're ending this awake, and you're keeping people close while you do.
cells.verb: charging toward what connects people, through feeling and shared meaning

cells.tense: You are living past the ending, in a version of it that has not happened yet.
cells.ask: Pick the one ending you've been pressing hardest on and do nothing about it for three days — let it keep its own timing.
cells.core:
You're pushing the ending faster than it can go. Somewhere ahead is the clean version — settled, the air clear, the new thing already started — and you're talking from there, pressing the people around you toward a finish line they can't see yet. The pressure is meant to help. It's costing you the connections you're trying to bring along.

What's real is quieter than what you're doing. The ending will happen; it doesn't need dragging. Let one piece of it stay unfinished this week and watch what actually moves on its own. When you stop forcing the timeline, the thing that needs to break still breaks — and the people you were gripping come back to you.
cells.sheetLine: You're rushing a finish that doesn't need rushing.

cells.tense: You are talking about it in present tense, as if the change were still ahead of you.
cells.ask: Write down what actually ended — five lines, no feelings — and show it to one person who wasn't there.
cells.core:
You describe that thing as if it were still live. The calls, the habit, the plan you were both holding — you speak about them in the present, bracing for a change that has already mostly run. So the clearing doesn't get to be done, and the goodbye stays unfinished in your mouth.

The missing piece is the shape of what happened, laid out plainly, the way you'd explain a problem to someone else. Naming the sequence is how you get to leave it. Tell one person the order of events, not the story. Say what came first, then what came next, then what stopped.
cells.sheetLine: You talk about it like it's still happening. It isn't.

cells.tense: You are clearing the room already, and calling it just how things go.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've quietly let end in the last month and say out loud that you chose it.
cells.core:
The ending is underway, and you're the one who made it happen. Somewhere in the last stretch you stopped feeding something — a connection, a habit, a version of a plan — and it went quiet, and you've been describing that as circumstances or drift. It wasn't drift. You made a call, and you're not taking credit for it.

The clearing is real and it's working. The piece left out is you standing behind it. When you call an ending an accident, nothing gets learned from it, and the people around you can't learn either. Own one of them — say it plainly to yourself first — and the same thing stops being something that happened to you and starts being something you can steer.
cells.sheetLine: You already let it end. You're calling it drift.
